title: The Carina Nebula imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
caption: The Carina Nebula, imaged by ESO's VLT Survey Telescope
celestial: Carina Nebula · constellation Carina · about 7500 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESO. Acknowledgement: VPHAS+ Consortium/Cambridge Astronomical Survey Unit

recognition.text: Ranked #12 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: This detailed picture from the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory shows the Carina Nebula, a star-forming region in the southern constellation of Carina.

Star-forming regions like this one are vast clouds of gas and dust where new stars are born. The young, hot stars then light up and sculpt the clouds around them, creating the mix of glowing gas and dark dust typical of such nebulae. The telescope captured the scene through several broad color filters and one tuned to the red glow of hydrogen, the most common element in these clouds.

Chile's then President, Sebastián Piñera, helped to take the image when he came to Paranal on 5 June 2012. It was then released on 6 December 2012, when the new telescope was inaugurated in Naples. The official caption says little about the nebula itself and presents the picture mainly as a first demonstration of the new survey telescope.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (61.82 x 66.34 arcminutes) and distance (7500 light years), the frame spans roughly 135 × 145 light-years. Its light set out about 7,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the OmegaCAM camera on the VLT Survey Telescope, using broad color filters plus a filter for hydrogen light. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
filters: 440 nm · Optical B (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
480 nm · Optical g (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
625 nm · Optical r (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
659 nm · Optical H-alpha (VLT Survey Telescope OmegaCAM)
understand.eye: Long exposures on a survey telescope gather much more light than the eye, so the faint gas appears far richer here than it would by eye.
